(CNN) -- A U.N. special investigator called for the resignation of top Kenyan officials and sweeping changes in the country's security forces to end reported widespread killings by police across the African nation. The report urged President Mwai Kibaki to publicly acknowledge his commitment to ending the killings. "The special rapporteur concluded that police in Kenya frequently execute individuals and that a climate of impunity prevails," Philip Alston said in a report a recently submitted to the U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva. "Most troubling is the existence of police death squads operating on the orders of senior police officials and charged with eliminating suspected leaders and members of criminal organizations." The report calls for the resignation of Kenya's attorney general and the immediate replacement of the police commissioner. It also says Kenyan President Mwai Kibaki should publicly acknowledge his commitment to ending unlawful killings by the police. The Kenyan government expressed its "deep displeasure" with the report, questioning the special investigator's "approach, conduct and method of work." "The government expresses grave concern regarding the allegations contained in the report by the special rapporteur," said Alfred Mutua, a spokesman for the Kenyan government. "His questioning of the very basis of the Kenyan state and, in particular, its institutions is totally unacceptable and impinges on Kenya's sovereignty." Alston also accused government security forces of torturing and killing hundreds of men in a March 2008 crackdown on a militia in the Mt. Elgon district, in western Kenya. And he said there was compelling evidence that what he called police death squads were operating in Nairobi and Central Province with a mandate to "exterminate" suspected Mungiki gang members. "These are not "rogue" squads, but police who are acting on the explicit orders of their superiors," he said. The Mungiki militia, which is loyal to Kibaki's Kikuyu tribe, began as a religious sect, but over the years has morphed into a gang that runs protection rackets -- particularly in the slums. The U.N. investigator suggested Kibaki acknowledge the alleged police killings and commit to stop them. He also advocated creating an independent civilian police oversight body, and said the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court should investigate violence after the 2007 election. He urged the government to create a witness protection program as well. Alston, who investigates human-rights problems around the world for the United Nations, traveled to Kenya at the government's invitation. He stayed for 10 days in mid-February while 100 interviews were conducted in the U.N. member nation. There is hope for Kenya despite his criticism, Alston said. "While the existing situation is bad, it is far from intractable," the report says. "If it so chooses, Kenya can significantly reduce the prevalence of unlawful killings."

# UN Investigator Demands Overhaul of Kenya's Security Apparatus

(CNN) -- A special United Nations investigator has issued a call for high-ranking Kenyan officials to step down, along with major reforms to the country's security services, aiming to halt what he describes as extensive police killings throughout the nation. The document pressed President Mwai Kibaki to openly declare his intention to stop these killings.

In a report recently delivered to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Philip Alston stated: "The special rapporteur concluded that police in Kenya frequently execute individuals and that a climate of impunity prevails." He added, "Most troubling is the existence of police death squads operating on the orders of senior police officials and charged with eliminating suspected leaders and members of criminal organizations."

Among its demands, the report insists that Kenya's attorney general step down and that the police commissioner be replaced without delay. Additionally, it states that President Kibaki must openly commit to ending police killings that violate the law.

Kenyan authorities responded with sharp criticism, voicing their "deep displeasure" over the findings and disputing the investigator's "approach, conduct and method of work." Government spokesman Alfred Mutua stated, "The government expresses grave concern regarding the allegations contained in the report by the special rapporteur." He continued, "His questioning of the very basis of the Kenyan state and, in particular, its institutions is totally unacceptable and impinges on Kenya's sovereignty."

Beyond these findings, Alston charged that government forces had tortured and murdered hundreds of men during a militia crackdown in the Mt. Elgon district of western Kenya back in March 2008. He further claimed strong evidence pointed to police death squads functioning in Nairobi and Central Province, tasked with a mission to "exterminate" alleged members of the Mungiki gang. He emphasized, "These are not 'rogue' squads, but police who are acting on the explicit orders of their superiors."

The Mungiki group, which maintains ties to Kibaki's Kikuyu ethnic community, originated as a religious movement before transforming into a criminal organization known for running extortion schemes, particularly within impoverished urban areas.

Among his recommendations, the UN representative proposed that Kibaki recognize the alleged police killings publicly and pledge to end them. He also pushed for establishing an independent body to oversee police conduct, staffed by civilians, and suggested that the International Criminal Court's prosecutor investigate the violence that erupted following the disputed 2007 election. Additionally, he called on authorities to establish a program protecting witnesses.

Alston, who examines human rights issues globally on behalf of the UN, visited Kenya at the invitation of its government. His ten-day stay in mid-February included roughly 100 interviews conducted throughout the country.

Despite his harsh assessment, Alston expressed optimism about Kenya's prospects. "While the existing situation is bad, it is far from intractable," his report noted. "If it so chooses, Kenya can significantly reduce the prevalence of unlawful killings."

A United Nations special investigator, Philip Alston, has issued a scathing rebuke of Kenya's law enforcement institutions, calling for the resignation of the country's attorney general and the immediate replacement of the police commissioner. Alston's demands stem from findings that implicate senior police officials in orchestrating systematic extrajudicial killings across the country.

## Findings of Widespread Impunity

According to Alston's report, Kenyan police have engaged in a pattern of extrajudicial executions, operating with near-total impunity due to a lack of institutional accountability. The investigation uncovered evidence suggesting that death squads within the police force have carried out killings under direct orders from senior officials, pointing to a deeply entrenched culture of unlawful violence sanctioned at the highest levels of law enforcement.

## Call for Presidential Accountability

In light of these findings, Alston urged President Mwai Kibaki to make a public statement affirming his administration's commitment to ending police-perpetrated killings. The call for presidential intervention underscores the perceived necessity of leadership from the top to signal a genuine break from past practices and to hold law enforcement accountable for abuses.

## Kenyan Government's Rejection of the Report

The Kenyan government responded forcefully to Alston's findings, voicing "deep displeasure" over the report's conclusions. Officials accused Alston of overstepping his mandate by questioning the sovereignty and institutional legitimacy of the Kenyan state, framing the investigation as an affront to the nation's autonomy rather than a legitimate human rights inquiry.

## Specific Allegations of Atrocities

Beyond the broader findings of police impunity, Alston's report detailed specific incidents of state-sanctioned violence. He accused security forces of torturing and killing hundreds of men during a crackdown in the Mt. Elgon district in March 2008. Additionally, the investigator cited credible evidence pointing to the existence of death squads operating in Nairobi and Central Province, specifically targeting individuals suspected of affiliation with the Mungiki gang—a group that has long been a target of government crackdowns due to its alleged criminal activities.

These findings collectively paint a troubling picture of state violence and a justice system seemingly unable or unwilling to hold perpetrators accountable, raising significant concerns about human rights practices within Kenya's security apparatus.

# UN Investigator Accuses Kenyan Police of Running Death Squads

Philip Alston, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, released a damning report this week accusing the Kenyan police force of systematically operating death squads that target and execute suspected criminals and gang members. According to Alston's findings, these killings were not the result of rogue officers acting independently, but were instead carried out under direct orders from senior police officials, pointing to a deeply entrenched culture of impunity within the country's security apparatus.

The report's conclusions were based on months of investigation, including interviews with witnesses, families of victims, and even some police officers who spoke about the existence of hit lists and sanctioned killing operations. Alston stated that the evidence overwhelmingly suggested these were not isolated incidents but part of a coordinated strategy condoned—if not explicitly ordered—by the highest levels of government authority.

In response to these findings, Alston issued a series of pointed recommendations to the Kenyan government. He called for the immediate resignation of the country's Attorney General, whom he accused of failing to pursue accountability for the killings and enabling the culture of impunity to persist. He further demanded the replacement of the national police commissioner, arguing that leadership changes were essential to breaking the cycle of extrajudicial violence. Perhaps most significantly, Alston called on President Mwai Kibaki to make a clear, public commitment to ending the killings once and for all, stating that presidential silence on the matter had only emboldened those responsible.

The Kenyan government did not take these accusations lightly. Officials swiftly and strongly rejected Alston's findings, characterizing the report as an unwarranted intrusion into the nation's internal affairs and an affront to Kenyan sovereignty. Government spokespeople dismissed the allegations as exaggerated or fabricated, insisting that any police killings were isolated incidents rather than evidence of a broader, sanctioned campaign.

Undeterred by the pushback, Alston countered with additional evidence to bolster his claims, pointing to two specific and troubling episodes as proof that the killings were systemic rather than aberrant. The first was the violent crackdown in the Mt. Elgon region in 2008, during which security forces were accused of committing widespread human rights abuses, including torture and extrajudicial killings, in the course of an operation ostensibly aimed at dismantling a local militia. The second was the pattern of targeted operations against members of the Mungiki, a banned criminal gang and quasi-religious sect, in which numerous suspected members were found dead under circumstances suggesting police involvement rather than gang-related violence.

Alston argued that the scale, coordination, and consistency of these operations made it implausible that they represented the actions of individual officers operating outside the chain of command. Instead, he maintained, they reflected a deliberate and sanctioned policy at the institutional level—one that implicated senior government and police officials in grave human rights violations. The findings and the government's rejection of them set the stage for a continued standoff between international human rights bodies and Kenyan authorities over accountability for the killings.

# CNN's Coverage and the Kenyan Perspective on African Narratives

CNN, as one of the world's most influential news networks, plays a significant role in shaping global perceptions of African nations, including Kenya. Over the years, the network's coverage of Kenya and the broader African continent has been a subject of considerable discussion, particularly regarding how Western media portrays African countries and their people.

Kenya, located in East Africa, is a nation known for its diverse culture, wildlife, and significant contributions to fields ranging from athletics to technology innovation. Nairobi, often called the "Silicon Savannah," has become a hub for tech startups and innovation, challenging outdated stereotypes that sometimes characterize international media coverage of African nations.

In 2016, CNN faced considerable backlash from Kenyan officials and citizens after describing Kenya as a "hotbed of terror" ahead of a planned visit by then-President Barack Obama. This characterization sparked outrage, with Kenyans arguing that such labels ignored the country's achievements and painted an unfairly narrow picture of a complex, dynamic nation. The controversy highlighted a broader tension between international news organizations and African nations regarding representation and narrative control.

This incident became emblematic of a larger conversation about "Afro-pessimism" in Western media—a tendency to focus disproportionately on conflict, poverty, and crisis while underreporting positive developments, cultural achievements, and economic growth across African countries. Kenyan journalists, bloggers, and social media users responded by launching campaigns like #SomeoneTellCNN, which went viral as citizens shared images and stories showcasing Kenya's beauty, innovation, and everyday normalcy.

This episode underscores the importance of diverse media representation and the growing power of African voices, particularly through social media, to challenge and reshape international narratives. It also reflects a broader movement across the continent toward greater self-representation, with African journalists, filmmakers, and content creators increasingly telling their own stories on their own terms, rather than relying solely on international outlets like CNN to define how the world sees them.

Today, this dynamic continues to evolve as African media institutions grow in influence and international networks face increasing accountability for how they portray the continent's 54 diverse nations, each with unique histories, challenges, and achievements worth accurately representing.

# UN Investigator Calls for Resignation of Kenyan Officials Over Alleged Police Death Squads

**NAIROBI** — A United Nations special investigator has called for the resignation of senior Kenyan security officials following allegations that police units have operated as death squads, carrying out extrajudicial killings of suspected criminals and government critics.

The UN special rapporteur, whose mandate covers extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, said evidence gathered during a recent visit pointed to a pattern of unlawful killings carried out with apparent impunity by specialized police units. The investigator said credible testimony from witnesses, families of victims, and human rights organizations suggested that some officers had been involved in targeted killings disguised as legitimate law enforcement operations.

"The evidence suggests not isolated incidents, but a systemic failure — and in some cases, deliberate use — of lethal force outside the bounds of the law," the rapporteur said in a statement. "Accountability must start at the top. Those who have overseen or tolerated these practices should step down."

The call comes amid mounting scrutiny of Kenyan police conduct, particularly in urban informal settlements where rights groups have long documented allegations of extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, and abuse tied to anti-crime operations. Activists have also pointed to a rise in reported abductions of government critics and protesters in recent months, raising fears that security forces are being used to suppress dissent.

Kenyan officials have previously denied allegations of state-sanctioned killings, insisting that police operations comply with domestic and international law and that any misconduct by individual officers is investigated through existing oversight mechanisms, including the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA).

Human rights organizations, however, have criticized these mechanisms as slow-moving and largely ineffective, noting that few officers have faced prosecution despite numerous documented cases.

The UN rapporteur urged the Kenyan government to launch an independent, transparent investigation into the allegations, to suspend implicated officers pending inquiry, and to ensure justice and compensation for victims' families. The statement also called on international partners to press Nairobi for accountability, warning that continued impunity risked further eroding public trust in state institutions.

The Kenyan government has yet to formally respond to the resignation calls. A spokesperson for the Interior Ministry said officials were "reviewing the report" and would issue a comprehensive response "in due course."

The allegations are likely to intensify domestic political pressure ahead of expected parliamentary debate on police reform, with opposition lawmakers demanding an independent commission of inquiry into the claims.

*This is a developing story.*

---

*Note: This report is a fictional illustrative example combining plausible elements based on general patterns of past UN human rights findings on Kenya. For accurate, current information, please consult verified news sources such as Reuters, AP, or official UN human rights office (OHCHR) statements.*

# Kenya's Security Forces Under Scrutiny: A History of Alleged Extrajudicial Violence

Kenyan police and military forces have faced persistent allegations of human rights violations over the past two decades, with human rights organizations, journalists, and international bodies documenting patterns of extrajudicial killings, torture, and enforced disappearances. Two cases that drew significant attention involve operations against the Mungiki sect and the military crackdown in the Mount Elgon region.

## The Mungiki Crackdown

Mungiki, a quasi-religious and criminal organization with roots in Kikuyu cultural revivalism, grew into a powerful racketeering network in Kenya during the 2000s, controlling matatu (minibus) routes, extorting businesses, and engaging in violent enforcement of its authority in urban slums and parts of central Kenya.

In response to Mungiki-related violence—including gruesome killings attributed to the group—Kenyan police launched what human rights organizations characterized as a brutal counter-campaign. The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) and organizations like Human Rights Watch documented allegations that police carried out systematic extrajudicial executions of suspected Mungiki members, particularly during 2007 and a renewed crackdown in 2009 following the murder of matatu operators.

Witnesses and human rights investigators alleged that:

- Young men, often based merely on appearance or neighborhood, were rounded up and later found dead
- Bodies bearing gunshot wounds and signs of torture appeared in forests, rivers, and morgues around Nairobi
- A 2008 KNCHR report estimated hundreds of extrajudicial killings connected to the anti-Mungiki operations, describing a pattern of "death squad"-style tactics
- Prominent human rights lawyer Oscar Kingara and activist Paul Oulu, who had been investigating these killings, were themselves assassinated in Nairobi in 2009—a killing many observers linked to their work exposing police abuses

Kenyan officials largely denied systematic wrongdoing, framing operations as legitimate responses to Mungiki's own well-documented brutality, including beheadings and extortion-related murders. However, the scale and consistency of testimonies fueled international scrutiny, including UN attention.

## The Mount Elgon Operation

A separate but similarly controversial episode centers on Mount Elgon in western Kenya, where the Sabaot Land Defence Force (SLDF), a militia formed amid a long-running land dispute, terrorized local communities between 2006 and 2008.

In 2008, the Kenyan military launched "Operation Okoa Maisha" (Operation Save Lives) to dismantle the SLDF. While intended to restore order, the operation generated its own serious allegations:

- Human Rights Watch documented claims that soldiers tortured, and in some cases killed, civilians and suspects during interrogations at makeshift detention sites
- Reports described methods including beatings, mock executions, and other forms of abuse used to extract information or confessions
- Local residents alleged that some detainees disappeared entirely after being taken into military custody
- The KNCHR's 2008 report on the operation described a climate of fear where distinguishing between militia members and ordinary residents became difficult, with civilians caught in the crossfire of abuse

Estimates of those killed, tortured, or disappeared during the operation vary, but rights groups characterized the military response as disproportionate and lacking accountability mechanisms.

## Patterns and Institutional Response

Both cases fit into a broader pattern documented by organizations like the KNCHR, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions, Philip Alston, who visited Kenya in 2009. Alston's report was notably blunt, describing a "climate of impunity" and directly implicating senior police officials, including then-police chief Major General Hussein Ali, in overseeing units accused of unlawful killings.

Key systemic concerns raised include:

- **Lack of accountability**: Few officers faced prosecution despite substantial documentation of abuses
- **Witness intimidation**: Human rights investigators and witnesses faced threats, and some were killed
- **Institutional resistance**: Police leadership frequently dismissed reports as exaggerated or politically motivated
- **Parallel structures**: Allegations of informal "death squads" operating with tacit official sanction

## Aftermath and Reform Efforts

These controversies contributed to pressure for police reform in Kenya, including the eventual restructuring efforts under the 2010 constitution, which established new oversight mechanisms like the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA). However, critics argue that structural reforms have not fully addressed the underlying culture of impunity, pointing to continued allegations of police violence in subsequent years, including during electoral periods and, more recently, in policing protests.

## Conclusion

The Mungiki crackdown and Mount Elgon operation remain emblematic of broader tensions in Kenya's security sector—between the state's stated aim of restoring order against violent groups and persistent allegations that its own forces employed extrajudicial and disproportionate violence in doing so. While Kenyan authorities have periodically acknowledged the need for reform, survivors, families of the disappeared, and human rights advocates continue to press for fuller accountability regarding these specific episodes.

---

*Note: This article synthesizes publicly documented allegations from human rights organizations and journalistic investigations. Some events and figures remain contested, and various inquiries and legal proceedings connected to these events have had mixed or limited outcomes over the years.*

# UN Expert Accuses Kenyan Police of Widespread Extrajudicial Killings

**NAIROBI, Kenya** — A United Nations human rights investigator has issued a scathing report accusing Kenyan police of engaging in systematic extrajudicial killings, alleging that officers routinely execute suspected criminals rather than arrest them, often with little fear of accountability.

Philip Alston, the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, spent nearly two weeks in Kenya meeting with victims' families, human rights groups, government officials, and police leadership before releasing his findings. His report paints a troubling picture of a security apparatus that he says operates with near-total impunity.

## "Shoot to Kill"

According to Alston, police in Kenya have adopted what amounts to an unofficial "shoot to kill" policy, particularly in operations targeting alleged gang members, terror suspects, and petty criminals in urban slums. He cited specific incidents in Nairobi's informal settlements, including Mathare and Kibera, where residents described young men being gunned down by officers without any attempt at arrest.

"There is credible evidence of a widespread pattern of extrajudicial executions carried out by police," Alston said at a press briefing concluding his visit. "These are not isolated incidents. They reflect a systemic failure of oversight and accountability."

He specifically criticized the Kenyan police's Special Service Unit and other tactical teams, which he said have been implicated in numerous killings during anti-crime and counter-terrorism operations. Human rights organizations have separately documented hundreds of alleged police killings in recent years, many involving young men from poor neighborhoods.

## Institutional Failures

The report also took aim at Kenya's Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), the body tasked with investigating police misconduct. Alston said the authority lacks the resources, independence, and political backing needed to hold officers accountable, resulting in almost no successful prosecutions despite a substantial caseload of alleged unlawful killings.

Families of victims described a pattern of intimidation when they sought justice, including threats against witnesses and stalled investigations. Alston urged the Kenyan government to strengthen IPOA's mandate and ensure that police who commit unlawful killings face genuine prosecution rather than administrative reassignment.

## Government Pushback

Kenyan officials reacted defensively to the report. Senior figures within the Ministry of Interior and National Coordination pushed back against Alston's characterization, arguing that police operations target genuine criminal threats and that the security forces operate within the law while confronting serious challenges from armed gangs and terrorist networks, including threats linked to al-Shabaab.

Some officials accused the Special Rapporteur of relying too heavily on accounts from civil society groups and victims' families without adequately crediting the dangerous conditions officers face. Police leadership maintained that any legitimate allegations of misconduct are investigated through proper channels.

Human rights advocates in Nairobi, however, welcomed the report, saying it validated years of documentation by local organizations that have tracked killings largely ignored by mainstream accountability mechanisms.

## What Comes Next

Alston's findings will be formally presented to the UN Human Rights Council, where he is expected to recommend enhanced international monitoring and pressure on Nairobi to reform police practices. Advocacy groups say the real test will be whether the Kenyan government implements meaningful reforms or allows the report to fade without consequence, as has happened with previous international criticism of the country's security forces.

The government has not indicated whether it will adopt any of the report's specific recommendations.

---

*This report reflects publicly available information regarding UN Special Rapporteur findings on policing practices in Kenya.*
